subject: hauntedDollhouse
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: haunted Victorian dollhouse.
Style: gothic.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a haunted Victorian dollhouse diorama as a static prop, aiming for a few hundred parts and a handful of textures, since scenery like this doesn't need joints—just carefully structured geometry built from known primitives.

For the design itself, I'm sketching an asymmetrical dollhouse with a cutaway front revealing furnished rooms, a steep mansard roof with a round turret and conical cap, bay windows, a wraparound porch, and a crooked chimney, all sitting on a base plinth. I'm working out real-world proportions—roughly a meter wide, half a meter deep, and over a meter tall including the roof—dividing it into ground floor, second floor, and attic levels, with one side open to show the haunted interior and the other side kept as an intact facade with doors and windows.

For the contents, I'm planning the wow details room by room: parlor with a glowing fireplace, portraits with eyes, chandelier, sofa, clock, and damask wallpaper over a checker floor; the hall with stairs, a door, a floating ghost and candle; upstairs a canopy bed, rocking horse, ghost child, cradle, and moonlit window; and the attic with cobwebs, a trunk, bat cards, and a crow, topped by a mansard roof with scale-painted slate shingles and dormers.

Outside I'm keeping it minimal since the house itself is the focus per the brief -- just a small dead tree, a bit of cobweb, maybe a tiny graveyard with a couple tombstones on an extended front plinth, plus a low path and gate so the open front view into the interior isn't blocked. I'm starting to lay out coordinates with the house centered and the plinth depth extended forward for these small yard details.

Now I'm working out the vertical layout: ground floor slab, second floor slab, attic room, and the mansard roof section, stacking up to a total dollhouse height of roughly 1.2 meters with chimneys and a weathervane on top, which feels proportionate for a width of 1 meter.

For the color palette, I'm settling on a gothic scheme — dark plum walls with painted board lines, aged bone trim, slate blue-grey roof scales, and accents of sickly green and blood-red against a moonlit black iron framework.

Now I'm sketching out the key SVG textures needed: a damask wallpaper for the parlor back wall, a faded moons-and-stars wallpaper for the nursery, ghostly portrait frames of a lady and gentleman with glowing eyes, and a pointed-arch gothic window with mullions and glow.

Continuing to plan ghosts (lathe-shaped bodies with sphere eyes rather than flat cards), plus bat, cobweb, and smoke wisp cards, while working out where the front door texture should go given the house's open front.

For the entryway, I'm leaning toward making the right narrow vertical section a closed-in hall with its own front wall holding the door and a window above, leaving the main left portion open to view the interior, with the turret placed asymmetrically on the left for that Victorian feel.

Deciding on a hybrid layout: left wing fully open across two floors plus attic under the roof, right wing closed with its own front facade (door, porch posts, pointed window, gabled roof) and a side wall with windows at x=0.5. I'll place the round turret outside the left wall, centered around x=-0.52, z=0.08, so it doesn't conflict with the open parlor.

Now adjusting the turret's exact position so it reads as a corner tower, slightly overlapping the open front area but not blocking much of the room view, with a plinth wide enough (roughly x -0.78 to 0.78) to support both the turret and main house. I'll place a dead tree near the right side wall at x≈0.65 for yard detail.

I'm now defining the core dimensions: wall extents, front/back depth, floor heights for ground, second floor, and attic, plus slab thickness between them. I'm setting up a helper function for building box geometry parts with position offsets, checking whether parts can be added without joints since this is a static, unarticulated model.

For wallpaper, I'll use textured planes rather than boxes so each wall gets its own texture facing the correct direction, with back walls facing +Z and side walls facing inward toward +X or -X depending on which wall they're on.

I'm designing the SVG patterns for each room's wallpaper, matching the viewBox aspect ratio to the actual wall panel dimensions and using repeated damask motifs for the parlor's dark green and burgundy texture.

Reconsidering the floor widths — the left wing feels too narrow for one room with furniture, so I'm reworking the house proportions, widening the open wing to about 0.75 units with the turret shifted to x=-0.6 to give the parlor contents (fireplace, portrait, clock, sofa) enough breathing room.

For the attic, I'm thinking of the roof as a gabled mansard profile that stays open at the front, like an extrusion in the z-y plane that leaves the attic room visible rather than fully enclosed.

I'm overcomplicating this roof geometry. Let me simplify to a mansard-style profile instead: a steep lower slope from the back eave up to a kink point, then a shallower upper slope toward the ridge, defining everything in the (z,y) cross-section.

Actually, a cleaner approach: give the back a sloped slab roof, add gable-end triangle walls at the left edge and at the x=0.19 partition, and let the right wing have its own front-facing gable roof. Leaving the front slope open on the left wing keeps that classic open-front dollhouse look, with the attic reading as a gable cross-section missing its front face.

I'm now working out the geometry for an A-frame structure: a back slope from the eave up to the ridge, with the front slope replaced by exposed timber rafters leading down to the front eave so the attic stays visible, plus a cross-gable over the right wing with its own ridge running perpendicular.

For the right wing, I'm placing its ridge slightly higher than the main one, with two sloped slabs meeting a triangular front gable face that has a pointed window cut into it, and making sure the main roof's back slope tucks underneath where the two rooflines intersect.

I'll give the main roof solid gable-end triangles at both x=0.19 and x=-0.55, with the cross-gable roof positioned separately on the right wing so its upper slope overlaps that wall triangle but stays visually coherent through the open attic front.

For simplicity, the right wing stays closed with two floors, its ridge running along z with a peak height of F2+0.36. The turret is a lathed octagonal cylinder rising from the plinth up past F2, topped with a conical roof and finial, with pointed glowing window planes placed around its sides, and it slightly overlaps the left wall of the house for a cohesive low-poly puppet look.

I'm adjusting the turret's position so it bulges outward past the exterior wall rather than poking into the room, shifting its center to clear the interior face, and letting it stick out slightly in front of the house. Now I'm laying out the interior room coordinates — defining the inner faces of the left wall, the partition, and the back wall so I can place wallpaper and ground-floor furnishings correctly.

For the floor, I'm planning a thin textured plane with a checkered marble pattern placed just above the plinth, making sure its orientation axis avoids degenerate alignment with the default up vector by specifying a custom up direction.

Actually, simpler to use a procedural paint function checking floor/ceiling parity of x and z coordinates rather than an SVG texture—no texture asset needed that way. I'm considering combining painted checker floors with SVG-based wallpaper textures like damask patterns, and possibly wainscoting rendered via SVG too, then starting to enumerate each room's contents by position, beginning with the ground floor's open wing boundaries.

Mapping out the wallpaper plane for the back wall and thinking through how to handle side walls without a dedicated texture—I'm considering reusing the same wallpaper texture at a different aspect ratio, or switching to a procedural paint function with horizontal stripes and a wainscot cutoff based on height for the left and partition walls.

Now I'm planning the fireplace: a stone surround box with a mantle, a dark recessed firebox, and glowing orange embers inside, positioned on the back wall with specific dimensions for the opening and surround depth.

I also want extruded flame shapes glowing orange, candles with flames on the mantle, and a gothic skull accent sitting among them. Above the fireplace I'm placing an ornate gilded frame with a portrait of a lady, considering how to add glowing green eyes separately so only the eyes emit light rather than the whole textured plane.

I'm also planning the grandfather clock against the left wall with a dark wood body, hood, and clock face texture (hands stuck at midnight for fun), plus figuring out where to place a sofa or armchair along the back wall relative to the fireplace and clock positions.

Next I'm adding a glowing gothic window texture plane on the back wall, and placing a Victorian purple velvet sofa in front of it with buttoned tufts, arms, and feet. For the floor, I'm sketching a round rug in front as a disc shape.

Now I'm planning the rug's burgundy and gold ring pattern using a distance-based paint function, plus a chandelier hanging from the ceiling with a chain, torus ring, and glowing candle flames arranged in a loop. I'm also considering adding a small side table with a candelabra, tea set, skull, and hourglass as additional decor.

For the tea table I'm designing a round top with a central stem and three feet, topped with a lathe-built teapot, cups, and a glowing candle in a holder. I'm also sketching out a ghost-builder function that creates floating spectral figures with a bell-shaped lathe body and wavy hem, planning to place them in the parlor, bedroom, and attic at different scales.

For the ghost's silhouette, I'm giving it a rounded skirt made of spike-like cones around the bottom instead of a smooth hem, with raised capsule arms and a simple decal-style face texture. I'm going with a pale mint glow color so they look softly luminous, with black oval eyes and mouth painted onto a transparent face texture.

I'm deciding to skip the complicated sphere-wrap texture mapping and instead place a thin plane with the painted ghost face in front of the lathed body at head height, positioned so it doesn't clip into the curved body surface.

Still defining lathe profile points...

Adding arms as raised capsules and spikes along the hem, with each ghost built from a lathe body, spikes, arms, and a face plane—about a dozen parts per ghost, all using the glow mesh helper. Now moving on to the ground-level right wing building, starting with the front facade.

For the ground floor, I'm constructing the door opening by building left and right piers plus a lintel above, with the door itself as a textured plane at the center. I'm applying board-and-batten siding in dark plum for the facade, and for the second floor I'm opting for a glowing textured window plane with a frame rather than cutting an actual opening in the wall.

Simplifying further, I'm making the right wing a solid block rather than modeling its interior, since the partition wall blocks any view inside anyway -- this saves on parts while still matching the facade dimensions.

For the porch, I'm planning a platform with posts, a small shed roof, steps, a railing with turned balusters, and gingerbread brackets, positioning it in front of the door with specific width and depth measurements.

Now I'm working out the porch roof as a tilted slab with a slate color, fascia trim featuring a scalloped gothic arch between the posts, plus steps leading down and the door texture design.

For the door, I'm planning a dark panel with iron hinges, a knocker, and a glowing gap, topped with a pointed-arch fanlight glowing green, framed by an extruded gothic arch outline — then adding a matching second-floor gothic window with bone-colored frame and glow plane for the right wing.

Writing arch outline geometry...

Still building the arch outline function...

I'm deciding to skip importing the OutlinePoint type and define my own local point type instead, since the export path is uncertain. For the frame, I'm planning to extrude the outer arch shape for the solid frame, then layer a transparent glass plane with an SVG texture clipped to the arch shape in front of it.

Writing SVG arch path...

Verifying the arc geometry...

I want to create a reusable lancet window helper so all pointed-arch windows (porch, gable, dormers, turret) share one consistent texture scaled uniformly by width, keeping the arch's height-to-width ratio fixed.

For side-wall windows I'll rotate the orientation and reuse the textured plane logic, defaulting the up-axis appropriately. I'm also considering a second texture variant with a moon-and-bat motif for interior back windows, versus the standard glowing greenish-yellow panes with dark mullions for the rest.

Tallying up textures needed: wallpapers for parlor and nursery walls, two window variants (lit and moon), portraits for the lady and man, a clock, a door, a ghost face, plus bat/web/smoke card textures -- landing around twelve total, maybe skipping tombstone text to keep the atlas manageable.

Now I'm planning the material palette: slate roof scales, siding, floor and stone textures, wood grain, wrought iron, moss, and dirt. For the second floor open wing, I'm placing the nursery wallpaper on the back wall and laying out a four-poster bed with canopy, drapes, and headboard against the left side.

I'm figuring out the bed's orientation—whether to run it along z with the head against the back wall, or along x with the head against the left wall so the side profile faces front, deciding dimensions and placement accordingly.

Going with the side-profile layout: head at the left wall with four posts at the corners, a sagging canopy top, torn curtain fabric at the sides, and maybe a ghostly figure hovering over the bed. I'm also considering a window with moonlight and curtains on the back wall, plus a rocking horse nearby.

For the rocking horse, I'll build it from a capsule body, a frustum head, crescent-shaped rockers extruded on either side, small spiky mane cards, and tiny glowing red sphere eyes for a creepy touch. I'm also thinking about hanging a gentleman's portrait on the back wall near the bed's headboard area, still figuring out exact placement.

Mapping out the back wall from -0.53 to 0.18, I need to fit the bed, window, and portrait without overlap -- settling on window around x=0.06 and portrait around x=-0.12 to x=-0.08, with the bed ending at -0.26 so there's room. I'm also considering adding a cradle and other nursery furniture like a toy chest or small dresser near the window.

Now I'm placing the remaining floor items: a rocking horse near the wall portrait, and a cradle positioned under the window using a boxy frustum shape with small rockers. For lighting I'm planning a single hanging oil lamp from the ceiling using a lathe shape with a glowing sphere, then moving on to the floor planks with wood grain striping and starting on the ceiling treatment.

For the attic, I'm working out the A-frame roof geometry—computing the floor height, ridge height, and slope angles for both the steep back slope and the shallower open front slope, positioning the ridge slightly off-center to keep the roof proportioned over the attic's depth.

I'm now extruding the triangular gable end walls at each end of the attic, working out the cross product to get the correct thickness direction along the x-axis so the walls sit properly centered.

For decoration, I'm planning a round bullseye window on the left gable—a glowing disc with dark cross mullions—plus attic contents like a glowing trunk, a creepy mannequin dress form on a stick, cobweb cards in the corners, and 3D hanging bats made of capsule bodies with membrane wings.

For the bats themselves, I'll build 3 hanging ones under the ridge—ellipsoid bodies, sphere heads with cone ears, two wrapped teardrop wing extrusions along the sides, and glowing red eyes—plus 2 flying bats outside near the turret using small flat card sprites instead of full 3D geometry.

Instead of using angled cards that complicate facing, I'll use a simple textured plane facing forward for the bats, which is cheap and fine since they're only viewed from the front.

Now I'm planning the rafters: five rod beams running from the ridge to the front plate, plus a horizontal collar tie crossbeam, and thinking through how the back slope of the roof should look when viewed from behind or the sides.

Working out the rotation math for the back slope slab...

I'm placing the slab center on the slope line with a small outward offset and extending the eaves slightly beyond, giving a total length of about 0.414+0.06, and working out the x-extent for the roof slab including overhang into the cross gable. For the right wing roof, I'm setting the ridge along z at x=0.37 with a peak height of 1.05, eaves offset by 0.03 on each side, giving a rise/run that works out to roughly a 59.7° slope.

Each roof slab is rotated about the z-axis by this steep angle, with one slope descending toward +x and the other ascending, so I'm computing the rotated x/y basis vectors to confirm both normals point upward and outward correctly. The front gable face of the right wing is a triangular wall section extruded with thickness, including a lancet window cutout, and I'm adding bargeboard trim as a zigzag extrusion along both roof slopes for the gingerbread trim detail.

Now I'm adding small pendant spikes hanging below the barge trim, a finial spike topped with a sphere at the gable peak, and a weathervane (leaning toward a crow silhouette with directional letters) at the main ridge, plus a brick chimney with a cap and smoke elements rising through the main roof.

Adding chimney pots, brick texture, and a second chimney on the right wing, then building an octagonal turret tower with trim rings, vertical shingle siding, and lancet window planes facing outward at a few angles.

Capping it with a conical roof, then placing the window planes outward along the turret's octagonal faces, accounting for the flattening versus a true cylinder.

Good, 0.05 window width fits within the 0.107 face width. I'll switch to using a flat-shaded 8-sided cylinder for the turret body, then design a gothic spire roof using a lathe profile with a curved bulge tapering up to a point.

Now I'm working out the plinth dimensions so it's wide enough to contain the turret, trying to keep everything roughly centered given the house spans and the turret's offset position.

I'm layering the plinth: a dark wood base box, a slightly larger overhang top plate, and a thin ground slab on top painted with mottled dead-grass colors to look like worn moss and earth.

For the yard, I'm placing flagstone path pieces leading from the porch steps to the front edge, then adding a wrought iron fence with a gate opening aligned to the steps, picket posts with finials, and spear-tipped pickets. To keep the part count manageable I'm merging the repeated picket and spear-tip geometries into single combined meshes using BufferGeometryUtils, since all the underlying box/cylinder/cone geometries share compatible attributes.

Rather than fencing the entire plinth perimeter, I'm limiting it to the front run plus two short return sections on the sides, with evenly spaced posts and a gap left open for the gate. Now I'm starting to lay out graveyard-style elements on the left side of the yard, beginning with a pair of rounded-top tombstones.

I'll skip the mailbox and moon ideas, sticking with the tree sweep with six branches and twigs. Before writing the final code, I should run through the builder API I'm relying on -- part, extrude, sweep -- to make sure I'm using correct signatures.

Then I'm considering importing the clockwork kit for brass/iron/gilt metal paints, maybe adding a visible gear train inside the grandfather clock's case for a nice detail touch.

I'll skip the exposed gear mechanism since the clock body is closed, and just use the metal() material from the clockwork kit along with glow, importing both from their respective kit paths. I'll also pull in the frame helper from the SDK and double-check the part syntax for applying textures with position and direction.

Scale options accept arrays like with the toon eye example, so I can scale spheres non-uniformly that way. I need to watch the flat-color limit of 64 — paints don't count toward it but plain string colors do, so I'm planning to define a reusable palette object and keep the total under roughly 45 to stay safe.

I'm defining core colors like ink black, bone, bone dark, and plum for siding, while reserving larger painted surfaces for more liberal color use since paint textures don't count against the limit. I'm estimating texel density for an 8 square meter painted area comes out fine at roughly 3mm resolution with a 2048 paint size.

Writing siding paint function...

Still writing siding shader...

Writing shingle paint function...

Settling on a simple rectangular shingle approach with a hash function for per-tile shading and slope direction vectors for each roof face, including the back slope and angled wings, now thinking about how the turret roof needs its own treatment.

For the cone turret, I'll use height along the roof for rows and the angle around the circle for columns, generalizing with a coords function that different roof shapes can plug into. Then I'll set up stone paint for the plinth, tombstones, and fireplace using mottled textures, and wood grain for other surfaces.

Now I'm sketching out the floor checker pattern, brick coloring for the chimney using row/column coordinates based on dominant normal direction, and wallpaper for interior walls. Starting to write the actual builder setup with helper functions for creating boxes and other geometry pieces.

Writing more geometry helpers...

Now I'm setting up the imports, pulling in the builder utilities and kit functions like glow and metal from the agentic-3js-builder package, then starting to sketch the actual constants and setup code.

I'm thinking through type safety concerns—avoiding unused imports and parameters since strict typechecking will flag them—and defining a simple vector type alias along with a seeded RNG function to drive deterministic randomness throughout the scatter and placement logic.

Now I'm setting up the core dimensional constants for the dollhouse: wall positions, floor heights, wall thickness, and ridge height, then working through the exact z-coordinates for the back wall and front facade to make sure inner and outer faces align properly between wings.

I'm placing the back wall with exterior siding and interior wallpaper offset slightly in front for a gap, sizing the ground floor wallpaper panel to fit the back opening dimensions. Then I'm working out the left wall placement, treating it as a box where both faces get painted—wallpaper showing through to the exterior side.

The exterior left wall is mostly hidden by the turret, so I'm making the paint depend on surface normal: interior-facing normals get wallpaper, exterior-facing get siding. I'm applying the same normal-based logic to the partition wall and simplifying the back wall to full siding since its interior is covered by a separate plane anyway.

Defining stripe pattern for wallpaper...

The attic floor height works out cleanly with this modulo, and the attic's left wall is a separate gable triangle so it's fine on its own. The floor slabs span the full width, with trim capping the front edge, and I need to decide how the top face is painted per floor (wood planks for the bedroom) versus the underside.

Sketching plank texture logic...

Then I'm adding a mottled cream-gray ceiling plaster with a water-stain noise effect, and routing edges through a combined slab paint function that applies dark trim at front-facing normals. I'm also working out how to split the right wing block and partition walls so the siding block starts cleanly without overlapping the partition geometry.

For the right wing, I'm deciding face orientation logic so the interior-facing normal gets wallpaper while exterior gets siding, mirroring the same treatment on the left wall. Then I'm placing lancet windows and a door on the right wing's facade and side wall across both floors, and considering whether to add windows to the back wall too even though the diorama is viewed from the front.

I'll skip duplicating back windows except for one plane matching the interior glow, keeping it simple. Now I'm adding Victorian trim details: corner boards at the wing edges, a belt course between floors, eave brackets under the roofline, a cornice on the left wall, and front proscenium posts along the open edges.

I'm also considering small gothic corner brackets—quarter-arch fretwork shapes—at the four corners of each floor's open front, as a decorative touch rather than full arch frames that might obscure the view.

Now I'm figuring out the exact positions for the front posts on each floor, deciding on bone and dark trim colors, and planning small details like cobweb cards tucked into corners using a simple triangular web texture.

For the cobwebs I'm placing a textured plane with the web's corner at top-left into the back-left corner of the room facing forward, then reusing the same texture rotated 90 degrees to fit the top-right corner instead of mirroring it.

For the attic I'll add webs on a gable end facing outward, plus some in room ceilings, and I'm considering using the same card system for hanging web strands and chimney smoke.

A thread-hanging spider felt like fun but probably unnecessary, so I'll skip that and move into structuring each room's furnishings as separate local functions. I'm starting with the ground-floor fireplace, positioning the stone jambs and lintel against the back wall.

Still writing fireplace details...

Adding a stone chimney breast above the mantle with a portrait placed on it, then populating the mantle with a small skull decoration and a pair of glowing candles in gold holders.

I'm skipping a clock and light-pool glow effects to keep things simple, instead designing the portrait as a gilded frame with a textured plane and small corner ornaments, positioned centrally above the mantle against the chimney breast.

For the eyes, I'll add tiny glowing green emissive planes at calculated offsets within the portrait texture to give the painting a classic "eyes that follow you" effect, then I'm considering whether to include a grandfather clock against the left wall, sized to fit beneath the ceiling height.

Now I'm detailing the clock itself: a base box, trunk, and hood with a gothic triangular pediment on top, a clock face plane mounted on the hood front, and inside the trunk a glass door revealing a glowing brass pendulum for an eerie touch.

Moving to other furniture, I'm placing a parlor chandelier hanging from the ceiling with a chain, a gilded iron ring holding six candle arms with glowing flames, and a central decorative drop. Then I'm laying out a sofa with a base, seat cushion, and rolled back positioned against the wall.

Now I'm building a sofa with capsule-shaped rolled arms, box-shaped armrests, small cone feet, and tufted buttons along the back, planning a mottled velvet paint texture in deep plum tones. I'm checking the sofa's placement against the back window to make sure its height doesn't awkwardly overlap the window's bottom edge.

I'm also laying out positions for other furniture: the fireplace spans roughly -0.42 to -0.24 in x, a window sits near -0.08, and the sofa fits neatly beside it. To the right, I'm planning a tall bookshelf with a frame, four shelves, and randomly sized books in a limited palette of four colors, merged by color to keep the geometry efficient, plus some cobwebs for atmosphere.

Now I'm placing a round tea table in front of the sofa with a small rug beneath it, and on the tabletop I'm adding a lathe-built teapot, cups, a candle holder with a glowing flame, and maybe a book -- with a ghost hovering just above the scene along with some spider webs and a skull for extra creepy detail.

I'm then positioning the first ghost near the bookshelf, carefully scaling and offsetting its height so it floats close to but doesn't clip the ceiling. Moving to the second-floor nursery wing, I'm laying out the back wall panel dimensions to match the parlor and beginning construction of the bed -- starting with thin cylindrical posts topped with sphere finials marking the head and foot corners.

Now I'm detailing the headboard as a gothic arch shape extruded along the vertical plane, defining its pointed outline and positioning it at the head of the bed, then adding the lower footboard box and a thin mattress slab in pale linen tones above it.

I'm layering a tattered crimson blanket over the lower portion, a rounded pillow capsule at the head, and a dark wood base frame beneath, then building the canopy structure with corner rods, a dark purple cloth panel overhead, and considering fringe details for the valance edge.

Still adding valance spikes and curtain geometry...

I'm placing a small floating child ghost near the bed and another near the ceiling, then adding the back window with a moon texture, flanking curtains, a sill and arch frame, a portrait on the back wall, and a rocking horse figure.

Still writing geometry for the rocking horse...

Still working out rocker and body geometry...

Still working out rocker positions and leg rod placements...

For the cradle, I'm thinking a tapered box shape with small rockers and a hood, placed near the window, maybe with two tiny glowing green eyes peeking out from inside for a creepy touch. For the bedroom I want to add a hanging lantern from the ceiling, suspended by a rod, to give some ambient glow to the space.

I'll build a reusable lantern function with a chain, cap, glowing body, bottom ring, so I can use it for both the bedroom and a porch lantern later. For the attic, I'm setting up the second floor slab with planks and shaping the roof slabs so their interior faces show dark wood boards while the exterior faces show shingles, distinguishing them by their surface normal direction.

Now I'm figuring out the gable end triangles -- positioning the left gable wall against the open attic interior with its wood board face visible, while the right side butts against the cross-gable roof's slope, keeping track of the exact vertex coordinates so the triangle bases align with the floor and roof ridge correctly.

Now I'm planning a glowing round window on the left gable exterior, with a circle glow plane in green, cross rods, and a torus frame ring, then moving on to defining the front rafter rods from the ridge.

Still writing rafter and collar tie geometry...

Now I'm thinking about attic contents: a trunk with brass straps and a glowing interior, a dress form mannequin with a draped veil, a hanging lantern near the ridge, and possibly a leaning arch-framed mirror or hanging bats for extra atmosphere.

I decide to add a tiny ghost peeking from the trunk and a big spiderweb across the right gable, plus a charming Victorian porcelain doll sitting on the trunk — built from a lathe dress, pale sphere head, hemisphere hair with ringlet spheres, tiny glowing eyes, and rod arms. Then I move on to the right wing, planning its closed porch, gable, and roof details.

I'm estimating part counts across all the rooms and elements — walls, parlor, bedroom, attic, facade, roofs, turret, yard, tree, ghosts, and bats — landing around 380 parts, comfortably under the 1000 limit, and I start thinking through helper functions to keep the code compact.

Writing helper definitions...

Since typechecking status is unclear, I'll sidestep the risk by deriving the color type directly from the `b.part` function signature itself rather than importing a possibly unexported type.

I'm defining a cylinder helper that wraps `CylinderGeometry` with top/bottom radii, height, segment count, color, and position, centered along the vertical axis.

Now I'm adding a sphere helper for balls and a flame helper using an extruded glow shape facing forward, plus a candle helper that places a wax cylinder with a flame on top.

For the lathe helper, I'm sketching the call signature, then moving into writing the texture SVGs—starting with a parlor wallpaper pattern using a repeating fleur-de-lis style motif in dark maroon tones.

Writing SVG pattern...

Still writing wall decor details... I'm also double-checking that the wainscot height ratio stays consistent with the proportions used on the side walls.

For the nursery, I'm planning pale blue-gray faded stripes with peeling star and moon motifs above a sickly green beadboard wainscot, generating the striped pattern programmatically.

Now I'm designing the lit arched window: an arch-shaped SVG viewBox clipped to a gradient glass panel in yellow-green tones, with dark lead mullions dividing the panes and a tracery circle near the top.

I'm also planning a trefoil shape plus silhouettes of curtains and maybe a ghostly figure at the sides, keeping the arch outline stroked darkly and thick enough to read at the final raster size, with everything outside the arch left transparent.

Next I'm sketching variants: a moonlit window version with an indigo sky, pale moon, and silhouettes of a branch and bat, then a portrait-of-a-lady tile with a dark gradient background and a figure.

Writing portrait and clock SVG code...

Now moving to the ghostface icon: dark tall oval eyes, an "O" mouth shape, kept non-glowing so it reads as a shadowed face. Then I'm sketching a bat silhouette with spread scalloped wings, small ears, and two red eye dots in a near-black fill.

For symmetry in the wings, I'm mirroring one half-path via a transform rather than hand-coding both sides, duplicating the path and flipping it with a scale transform so it stays reliable across SVG renderers.

Now I'm thinking through a corner web design: radial strands fanning from the corner apex plus curved cross-threads at increasing radii, with stroke widths calculated carefully so they survive rasterization and alpha values kept above the cutoff threshold so the lines don't disappear.

For smoke, I'm layering overlapping puff ellipses in a dark lavender-gray that grow upward into a plume, with a pale greenish highlight to suggest a haunted chimney. I'm also mentally tallying the full texture list I need to produce: parlor, nursery, lit window, moonlit window, lady, man, clock, door, ghost face, bat, and more.

Now I'm planning out the paint definitions for each material: fish-scale shingles for the turret, custom shingle patterns for the roof, mottled stone and ground textures, wood grain for the plinth and dark wood, a custom brick pattern, metallic finishes for iron, tarnished brass, and gilt, plus velvet, checkered floors, plank floors, rugs, ceilings, and a mossy mottled tombstone texture.
